endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Define acceptable use policies for GAI interfaces, modalities, and human-AI configurations (i.e., for chatbots and decision-making tasks), including criteria for the kinds of queries GAI applications should refuse to respond to.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Is non-retaliation explicitly stated in the policy and in the reporting interface itself, covering demotion, dismissal, harassment, and other adverse actions?

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether a written non-retaliation policy increases reporting of AI-related concerns, and no study documents how often fear of retaliation suppresses such reports. Support for the recommendation rests on two governance frameworks, and only one of them addresses non-retaliation directly.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsements are expert framework guidance rather than empirical findings, so they do not change the rating. The size of the problem and the effect of a policy both remain unmeasured in this body of evidence.

The CHAI playbook asks whether non-retaliation appears in both the policy and the reporting interface, and whether it covers demotion, dismissal, harassment, and other adverse actions. The NIST Generative AI Profile excerpt addresses acceptable use policies and query refusal criteria. It does not mention retaliation, so it offers indirect support for this recommendation at most.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI concern reporting rates, report content, and time to resolution before and after a written non-retaliation policy is adopted, preferably with comparison sites. Surveys of staff, patients, and vendors could measure how often fear of retaliation deters reports about AI tools. Such surveys would establish whether the hazard exists at a meaningful rate.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Nothing is known about whether patients in these groups would learn of, understand, or trust a non-retaliation policy. Nothing is known about whether translated or plain-language versions would change their willingness to report AI-related concerns.
